title: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife
summary: Conservation organizations failed to substantiate imminent injury to members who wished to revisit distant endangered-species habitats; the Court rejected the standing theories on the summary-judgment record.
notes: Justice Scalia's opinion states the three constitutional elements (injury in fact that is concrete and particularized and actual or imminent; a causal connection fairly traceable to the challenged action; likely redressability) and rejected the members' 'some day' intentions to return as insufficient; Justice Stevens concurred only in the judgment, and Justice Blackmun's dissent was joined by Justice O'Connor.

sections.Parties: The respondents were organizations dedicated to wildlife conservation and related environmental causes. They sued the Secretary of the Interior over the geographic reach of Endangered Species Act consultation requirements. Members Joyce Kelly and Amy Skilbred supplied the individual-interest evidence discussed in the excerpt.
sections.Material Facts: Section 7 required federal agencies to consult to avoid jeopardizing listed species or critical habitat. A 1978 regulation applied consultation to actions in foreign nations; the later challenged interpretation limited it to the United States and high seas. Kelly had visited Nile crocodile habitat in Egypt, and Skilbred had visited endangered-species habitat in Sri Lanka. They hoped to return, but the evidence did not identify concrete plans for visits affected by the challenged projects. Skilbred acknowledged uncertainty about when she would return, partly because of civil war. The organizations also proposed ecosystem, animal, and vocational connections as bases for standing.
sections.Procedural History: The district court initially dismissed for lack of standing, and a divided Eighth Circuit reversed. The Supreme Court reached standing alone. Scalia’s opinion had Court support for Parts I, II, III-A, and IV; Part III-B had only four justices. The assigned pages reproduce principally the injury analysis, Kennedy’s partial concurrence, and Blackmun’s dissent.
sections.Issue: Whether past visits, indefinite intentions to return, or broad ecological and professional interests established a sufficiently personal and imminent injury from the revised consultation rule on the summary-judgment record.
sections.Holding: The organizations failed to show that their members were among those imminently injured. The Court did not decide whether the Secretary’s geographic interpretation of the statute was correct. The excerpt’s injury holding does not make the four-justice Part III-B analysis a controlling majority rule.
sections.Reasoning: The Court accepted observation of wildlife as a cognizable interest but demanded specific facts connecting the challenged activity to these members’ prospective injury. Prior visits and an unspecified desire to return did not establish imminent impairment. Broad theories reaching anyone interested in a species anywhere in the world lacked the necessary connection to the particular threatened animals or area. Kennedy, joined by Souter, agreed that this record was insufficient but would not categorically foreclose similar nexus theories under different facts. Blackmun, joined by O’Connor, argued that the majority confused the summary-judgment requirement to identify genuine factual disputes with an obligation to prove ultimate injury. He thought the members’ prior visits, professional interests, and stated intentions could support a factfinder’s inference of return. The disagreement therefore concerns both the substantive relation to threatened resources and the evidentiary showing appropriate at that stage.

topics.lrs-n-standing-injury: Indefinite future visits did not establish imminent personal injury on the supplied evidence.
topics.lrs-n-standing-constitutional: The opinion applies standing at summary judgment and divides over the proper evidentiary demand.
topics.lrs-n-standing-generalized: Part III-B rejected the citizen-suit theory as a generalized grievance that Congress cannot convert into an Article III case.
topics.lrs-n-standing-public-enforcement: The Court held the ESA citizen-suit provision could not confer standing on plaintiffs without concrete injury.
topics.lrs-n-standing-procedure: Footnote 7 explains when a procedural-right plaintiff may sue without meeting ordinary imminence and redressability standards.
